stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26 year old man in the early psychosis clinic. He presented 12 weeks ago with a first episode of psychosis and started olanzapine 10 mg nightly. His positive symptoms have fully remitted, he has returned to his apprenticeship and he is keen to stay on the current treatment.

He has gained 7 kg since starting and his waist circumference has risen from 89 cm to 104 cm. He has no family history of diabetes and no personal history of an eating disorder. His fasting bloods were taken this morning after a documented 10 hour fast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 128/80, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (less than 42); triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7)
data_table.Blood tests: Renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence metformin alongside a structured diet and exercise program
options.rationale: Metformin has the strongest evidence of any pharmacological agent for attenuating antipsychotic associated weight gain and dysglycaemia, and it addresses the impaired fasting glucose without destabilising a first episode responder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Switch olanzapine to aripiprazole with a cross taper over four weeks
options.rationale: Switching lowers metabolic risk but carries a real relapse hazard in the first year after a first episode, so it is reserved for when metabolic measures fail rather than being the opening move in a full responder (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Refer to a dietitian for review and repeat the panel in twelve months
options.rationale: Lifestyle referral alone leaves an established impaired fasting glucose untreated, and a twelve month interval is far longer than the three monthly review this trajectory warrants (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Commence orlistat and arrange fasting lipids again in three months
options.rationale: Orlistat has weak and inconsistent evidence in antipsychotic associated weight gain and does not improve glycaemia, which is the abnormality driving the decision here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg nightly and continue current lifestyle advice
options.rationale: Olanzapine weight gain is not reliably dose proportional in the therapeutic range, so halving the dose sacrifices relapse protection without dependably reversing the metabolic trend (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Metabolic screening is scheduled at baseline, at 3 months and then at least annually for anyone on a second generation antipsychotic, with olanzapine and clozapine carrying the highest liability. The 3 month panel is the point at which most weight gain has already occurred, which is why it is an action point rather than a data point. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of the roughly 15 year mortality gap in schizophrenia, so metabolic abnormalities are treated with the same seriousness as in any other patient. Relapse risk in the first year after a first episode is high enough that agent switching is weighed carefully against metabolic gain.
key_points: Metabolic screening at baseline, 3 months, then at least annually on second generation antipsychotics
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest weight and dysglycaemia liability
Metformin is the best evidenced pharmacological adjunct for antipsychotic associated weight gain
Switching agents in a first episode full responder risks relapse and is not the first metabolic move
explanation.pearls: Most olanzapine associated weight gain happens in the first 12 weeks, so the 3 month metabolic panel is the window where metformin changes the trajectory rather than merely documenting it.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of childbearing potential
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 23 year old woman in the outpatient clinic. She has bipolar I disorder and has been euthymic for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, after two admissions for mania in her late teens.

She tells you she married three months ago and hopes to conceive within the next year. She is using no contraception. She has never taken lamotrigine or lithium, and she has had no depressive episodes. Her most recent valproate level, full blood count and liver function are within normal limits.

data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily; no other regular medicines
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate within therapeutic range; full blood count, liver function and beta human chorionic gonadotropin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and start high dose folate 5 mg daily
options.rationale: High dose folate does not offset valproate teratogenicity, and it does nothing about the dose dependent neurodevelopmental harm, so it cannot substitute for changing the agent (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Halve the valproate dose now and review her mood state again in three months
options.rationale: Teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk persists at lower doses even though it is dose related, so a half dose leaves her both exposed and less well protected against relapse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange reliable contraception and cross titrate valproate to an alternative agent
options.rationale: Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless no alternative is tolerated and pregnancy is reliably prevented, so cover with contraception while a planned switch is completed before conception is attempted (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cease valproate today and review her again once she has a positive pregnancy test
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of an effective mood stabiliser in bipolar I invites relapse, and deferring the decision to a confirmed pregnancy means organogenesis has already occurred by the time she is reviewed (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Maintain valproate and refer for detailed foetal morphology once she conceives
options.rationale: Morphology imaging detects structural malformation but cannot detect the neurodevelopmental impairment that is the dominant valproate harm, so surveillance is not a substitute for avoidance (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Valproate exposure in pregnancy carries roughly a 10 per cent risk of major congenital malformation and up to a 30 to 40 per cent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment, both substantially higher than any other mood stabiliser. Australian regulatory advice restricts its use in women who could become pregnant to those in whom alternatives have failed and who are covered by reliable contraception with documented counselling. The switch itself takes months to complete safely in bipolar I, which is why the conversation belongs well before conception rather than at the first positive test. Lamotrigine is a common destination when the illness course is depression predominant, while lithium is often preferred when mania has dominated.
key_points: Valproate carries about 10 per cent major malformation risk and up to 30 to 40 per cent neurodevelopmental impairment risk
Restricted in women of childbearing potential to failure of alternatives plus reliable contraception
Folate supplementation does not mitigate valproate specific teratogenicity
Cross titration to an alternative takes months and must precede attempted conception
explanation.pearls: Neural tube closure completes by about day 28 after conception, which is often before a period is even missed, so a switch planned only after a positive test has already missed the window it was meant to protect.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

stem:
You are the registrar in a community mental health team reviewing a 41 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for six years with good symptom control and normal neutrophil counts throughout.

He smokes 25 cigarettes a day and has decided to stop entirely from next Monday, having been accepted into a quit program. He asks whether anything needs to change. He takes no other regular medicines, drinks no alcohol and has had no recent illness or dose change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/74, RR 15, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 450 mg daily in divided doses
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); renal function and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Make no change to clozapine and review his mental state again in three months
options.rationale: Doing nothing ignores a predictable pharmacokinetic rise in clozapine concentration after cessation, which can produce sedation, seizures and myocarditis like presentations within days (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Increase clozapine by 100 mg daily to offset the loss of a nicotine effect
options.rationale: This reverses the direction of the interaction, since stopping smoking removes enzyme induction and raises rather than lowers clozapine concentrations (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Substitute nicotine replacement therapy indefinitely to keep the interaction stable
options.rationale: The induction is caused by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke rather than by nicotine, so nicotine replacement does not preserve the interaction and would commit him to indefinite therapy for no pharmacokinetic gain (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Withhold clozapine on the quit date and restart at the same dose after one week
options.rationale: An interruption beyond about 48 hours requires full retitration from a low dose because of the risk of cardiovascular collapse on resumption, so a planned week off is unsafe (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Measure the clozapine plasma level and plan a staged dose reduction as he stops
options.rationale: Loss of cytochrome P450 1A2 induction on cessation raises clozapine concentrations by roughly 50 to 70 per cent over one to two weeks, so a baseline level with staged reduction and repeat monitoring is the standard approach (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Tobacco smoke induces cytochrome P450 1A2 through polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and clozapine and olanzapine are the psychotropics most affected. Cessation removes that induction over roughly one to two weeks, so a stable dose becomes an effectively higher exposure without any prescribing change. The same effect occurs abruptly when a smoker is admitted to a smoke free hospital ward, which is a common and under recognised precipitant of clozapine toxicity. Conversely, a patient who resumes heavy smoking after discharge can fall to subtherapeutic concentrations and relapse.
key_points: Tobacco smoke, not nicotine, induces cytochrome P450 1A2
Cessation raises clozapine concentrations by about 50 to 70 per cent over one to two weeks
Admission to a smoke free ward reproduces the same interaction abruptly
Clozapine interrupted for more than about 48 hours needs full retitration from a low dose
explanation.pearls: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for quitting in schizophrenia and does not itself affect clozapine concentrations, so the dose adjustment is driven purely by the loss of smoke induced enzyme induction.

subtopic_detail: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with comorbid depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29 year old accountant referred with lifelong inattention, disorganisation and difficulty completing tasks. School reports from age eight describe the same pattern, and a structured assessment supports a diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Over the past four months he has also had persistent low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking and passive thoughts that life is not worth living, with no plan or intent. He has never taken psychotropic medication. He drinks two standard drinks weekly and uses no other substances. His thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, reactive but predominantly low affect, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment approach?

options.text: Start lisdexamfetamine and add an antidepressant only if his mood fails to lift
options.rationale: Stimulants do not reliably treat a major depressive episode and can worsen the sleep disturbance and agitation already present, so leading with them leaves the more dangerous condition untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Treat the depressive episode first and reassess the attention symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: The more severe and more acutely risky condition is treated first, and depression itself impairs concentration, so the true attention deficit burden can only be gauged once mood has responded (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Start atomoxetine and lisdexamfetamine together to cover both symptom clusters
options.rationale: Combining two agents for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder at initiation is not standard practice and neither drug is an established treatment for a major depressive episode (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Offer psychological skills coaching alone and review his progress in six months
options.rationale: Coaching addresses the executive function difficulties but leaves a moderate depressive episode with passive suicidal thoughts untreated for an unacceptably long interval (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Decline to diagnose attention deficit disorder until his mood has been in remission
options.rationale: The developmental history from age eight already establishes the diagnosis, so withholding it is unnecessary even though the current symptom severity cannot be judged during a depressive episode (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in adults is commonly comorbid with mood and anxiety disorders, and sequencing treatment matters because each condition distorts the assessment of the other. The general rule is to stabilise the condition that carries the greater immediate risk, which here is a depressive episode with passive suicidal ideation. Once mood improves, residual inattention can be measured against the developmental baseline and stimulant therapy considered on its merits. Stimulant prescribing in Australia is also regulated by state and territory authorities and generally requires an authority to prescribe, which adds a practical reason to sequence rather than start everything at once.
key_points: Comorbid mood and anxiety disorders are the rule rather than the exception in adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Depression independently impairs concentration and inflates apparent attention deficit severity
Treat the condition with the greater immediate risk first
Childhood evidence of symptoms is required for the diagnosis and is not invalidated by current depression
explanation.pearls: Symptoms must have been present before age 12 for an adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosis, so a school report is often more diagnostically decisive than anything observed in the consulting room.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Post traumatic stress disorder in a refugee patient
stem:
You are the registrar in a community mental health clinic seeing a 34 year old man who arrived in Australia two years ago on a humanitarian visa. He describes nightly nightmares, intrusive daytime images of events during his detention overseas, avoidance of news broadcasts and constant scanning of his surroundings.

Symptoms have been present for 14 months and he now sleeps about four hours a night. His preferred language is Dari and a professional interpreter is present. He describes no hallucinations outside the intrusive imagery, no elevated mood and no substance use. He is housed, has permanent residency and is not facing any visa determination.

data_table.Examination: Hypervigilant, startles at corridor noise, mood anxious with congruent affect, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence prazosin at night and review the frequency of his nightmares in a month
options.rationale: Prazosin targets nightmares specifically and is an adjunct rather than a first line treatment for the whole disorder, so it leaves the intrusion and avoidance clusters unaddressed (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: Commence quetiapine at night given the severity of his sleep disturbance
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not recommended as monotherapy for post traumatic stress disorder and carry metabolic risk without evidence of benefit on the core symptom clusters (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: Commence sertraline and arrange a further medical review again in four weeks
options.rationale: Sertraline is an effective second line option or an adjunct, but Australian guidance places trauma focused psychological therapy ahead of medication when therapy is available and acceptable (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: Refer for trauma focused psychological therapy delivered with an accredited interpreter
options.rationale: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing are the first line treatments for established post traumatic stress disorder, and working through an accredited interpreter preserves that evidence base rather than diluting it (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: Provide supportive counselling and psychoeducation and reassess him in three months
options.rationale: Non trauma focused supportive counselling is consistently less effective than trauma focused therapy in established disorder, and 14 months of symptoms means watchful waiting has already been tried by default (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

explanation.summary: Australian guidance places trauma focused psychological therapy ahead of pharmacotherapy as first line treatment for post traumatic stress disorder, with medication reserved for patients who decline therapy, cannot access it, or fail to respond. Refugee patients were historically excluded from trauma focused therapy on the assumption that ongoing stressors made it unsafe, but the evidence now supports offering it once basic safety and settlement needs are met. Ongoing visa insecurity, homelessness or active threat are genuine reasons to sequence stabilisation first, and none of those apply here. Specialist torture and trauma services exist in every Australian state and can deliver therapy with trained interpreters.
key_points: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy and eye movement desensitisation are first line for established post traumatic stress disorder
Medication is second line or adjunctive when therapy is available and acceptable
Refugee status is not a contraindication to trauma focused therapy once settlement is secure
Prazosin is a nightmare specific adjunct, not a whole disorder treatment
explanation.pearls: Use an accredited interpreter rather than a family member for trauma histories, because relatives are frequently part of the traumatic narrative and their presence reliably suppresses disclosure.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic. Your patient is a 33 year old man with schizophrenia who is currently well, working part time and taking paliperidone. He has full decision making capacity on assessment today.

His mother telephones the clinic. She says he has stopped answering her calls, has been awake all night for a week and has been talking about neighbours reading his thoughts. She asks you what medication he is on and whether his dose has changed. Your patient told you at his last visit that he does not want his family given any information about his care, and he has not repeated or withdrawn that instruction.

data_table.Examination: At last review two weeks ago: euthymic, no delusions elicited, insight preserved, capacity intact
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone long acting injection, dose unchanged for eight months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the mother's call?

options.text: Record her account in full and explain that you cannot disclose his clinical details
options.rationale: Receiving information from a carer is not a disclosure and is always permissible, while releasing details about his treatment without consent would breach confidentiality in a patient with capacity who has expressly refused (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles).
source_refs: RANZCP Code of Ethics
Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles

options.text: Tell her the medication name and dose because she is his nominated primary carer
options.rationale: Carer status alone does not create a right of access to clinical information when an adult with capacity has refused consent, and no exception applies on the facts given (Source: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles).
source_refs: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles

options.text: Decline the call entirely and advise her to raise her concerns with her son directly
options.rationale: Refusing to take collateral information discards clinically important relapse data and confuses a duty not to disclose with a non existent duty not to listen (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).
source_refs: RANZCP Code of Ethics

options.text: Disclose his details on the basis that a relapse constitutes a serious imminent threat
options.rationale: The serious and imminent threat exception permits only the minimum disclosure necessary to lessen that threat, and the described relapse features do not yet meet that bar (Source: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles).
source_refs: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles

options.text: Ask her to obtain his written consent before you will accept any further information
options.rationale: Making consent a precondition for accepting collateral inverts the rule, since consent governs what leaves the clinic rather than what comes in (Source: RANZCP Code of Ethics).
source_refs: RANZCP Code of Ethics

explanation.summary: Confidentiality restricts what a clinician discloses, not what a clinician may receive, and this asymmetry is the single most useful principle in carer interactions. A carer can always give collateral history, and that history should be documented and acted on clinically, including by bringing the patient forward for review. Disclosure without consent requires a specific legal basis such as a serious and imminent threat to health or safety, an authorisation under the relevant state mental health legislation, or a nominated support person provision. Clinicians can also offer generic information about the illness, services and carer support without disclosing anything patient specific.
key_points: Receiving collateral from a carer never requires patient consent
Disclosing clinical details about an adult with capacity does require consent or a legal exception
The serious and imminent threat exception permits only the minimum disclosure needed
Generic illness and service information can always be offered to carers
explanation.pearls: Ask patients while they are well to nominate what may be shared and with whom, because a documented advance instruction converts this dilemma into a simple lookup at the moment of relapse.

sources.label: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner Australian Privacy Principles

stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38 year old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking what her partner estimates was about 30 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets. She is drowsy but rousable and answers questions.

Her pupils are 6 mm and sluggish and her mouth is dry. Her blood pressure has been stable since arrival and she has had no seizure. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.36. Serial electrocardiograms show the QRS duration lengthening from 96 ms on arrival to 118 ms now, with a terminal R wave in lead aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 112/70, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13, dry mucous membranes, pupils 6 mm sluggish, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: QRS 118 ms with terminal R wave in aVR; venous pH 7.36; paracetamol not detected; potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g orally now that she is able to answer questions
options.rationale: Charcoal is of limited value beyond one hour and carries an aspiration risk in a patient with a falling conscious level, so it does not take precedence over treating cardiac sodium channel blockade (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes and repeat the tracing
options.rationale: Magnesium treats torsades de pointes arising from QT prolongation, whereas the lethal mechanism here is QRS widening from fast sodium channel blockade, which magnesium does not reverse (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol as a bolus and reassess the tracing
options.rationale: A QRS above 100 ms signals sodium channel blockade and predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia, and hypertonic sodium bicarbonate is the specific antidote through combined sodium loading and alkalinisation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology
Austin Health Toxicology Handbook

options.text: Give intravenous lipid emulsion 20 per cent at 1.5 mL/kg and observe for one hour
options.rationale: Lipid emulsion is a salvage measure reserved for cardiac arrest or refractory instability after bicarbonate has failed, not an intervention for a patient who is still perfusing (Source: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).
source_refs: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil 200 mcg and titrate against her conscious state
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines rather than tricyclics, and it lowers the seizure threshold in a patient already primed for tricyclic induced seizures (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology

explanation.summary: Tricyclic toxicity kills through fast sodium channel blockade producing QRS widening, ventricular arrhythmia and cardiovascular collapse, with anticholinergic and alpha blocking effects layered on top. The electrocardiogram is the risk stratification tool rather than the drug level, and QRS duration above 100 ms predicts seizures while duration above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. Hypertonic sodium bicarbonate works by two mechanisms at once, increasing extracellular sodium to overcome channel blockade and raising pH to reduce drug binding to the channel. Hyperventilation to a similar target pH is an adjunct in the intubated patient, and hypotension refractory to bicarbonate and fluid is managed with noradrenaline rather than further alkalinisation.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms predicts seizures and above 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia
A terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm is a supportive marker of sodium channel blockade
Sodium bicarbonate works by sodium loading and alkalinisation together
Flumazenil is contraindicated because it lowers the seizure threshold
explanation.pearls: Aim for an arterial pH of about 7.50 to 7.55 with bicarbonate boluses repeated against serial QRS duration, and treat any tricyclic seizure with a benzodiazepine because phenytoin shares the sodium channel blockade that is causing the problem.

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and the lorazepam challenge
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to review a 57 year old woman on a medical ward. She was admitted three days ago with reduced oral intake. Over the past week she has become mute, holds her left arm in whatever position it is placed, and resists passive movement of her neck.

She has a history of severe depression and was started on olanzapine 10 mg nightly by her general practitioner two weeks ago. She has not eaten for 48 hours. Her creatine kinase is 180 U/L, she has been afebrile throughout, and there is no rigidity in her lower limbs or autonomic instability.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility of the left arm, negativism on neck movement, staring, no lower limb rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (30-190); white cell count, renal function and calcium within normal limits; computed tomography of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg nightly and review her presentation again tomorrow
options.rationale: Escalating an antipsychotic in catatonia risks precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which shares underlying pathophysiology, and antipsychotics are the agents most likely to worsen the syndrome (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Commence dantrolene and bromocriptine and transfer her to a high dependency bed
options.rationale: These agents treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is excluded here by a normal temperature, a normal creatine kinase and absent autonomic instability (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Arrange an urgent electroencephalogram before commencing any psychotropic treatment
options.rationale: Non convulsive status epilepticus is worth excluding when the picture is atypical, but the bedside signs here are specific enough that a therapeutic trial is both diagnostic and faster (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and refer her for daily psychology
options.rationale: Antidepressants do not treat acute catatonia and take weeks to act, which is far too slow for a patient who has not eaten for 48 hours (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cease olanzapine and give a lorazepam challenge with a planned response assessment
options.rationale: Waxy flexibility, mutism and negativism define catatonia, and a lorazepam challenge is both the diagnostic test and the first line treatment while the offending antipsychotic is withdrawn (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis and occurs most often in mood disorders, then in psychotic disorders and in general medical conditions including autoimmune encephalitis. It is frequently missed on medical wards where mutism and immobility are attributed to depression, delirium or non compliance. The lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic at once, with a partial response within 10 to 30 minutes supporting the diagnosis, and non response is not sufficient to exclude it. Untreated catatonia progresses to dehydration, pressure injury, venous thromboembolism and malignant catatonia, and electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment when benzodiazepines fail or the presentation is malignant.
key_points: Catatonia most commonly complicates mood disorders rather than schizophrenia
Normal temperature and normal creatine kinase argue against neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Antipsychotics can precipitate malignant catatonia and are generally withdrawn
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when benzodiazepines fail or the picture turns malignant
explanation.pearls: A lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg intravenously produces partial relief of mutism or posturing within 10 to 30 minutes in the majority of catatonic patients, and paradoxical alerting rather than sedation is itself a positive result.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar disorder with psychotic features
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman with a four year history of recurrent illness, using her complete case notes and a collateral history from her sister.

She has had two manic episodes with grandiose delusions and one depressive episode with nihilistic delusions, and each set of psychotic symptoms resolved as the mood episode resolved. Between the second and third episodes she had a nine week period documented at weekly reviews in which she remained convinced that a broadcaster was inserting thoughts into her mind, while her mood ratings, sleep and energy were consistently recorded as normal and she continued working full time. She uses no substances and her urine drug screen and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Currently euthymic, no delusions elicited today, insight partial
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; thyroid function, full blood count and renal function within normal limits; magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood congruent psychotic features occurring during episodes
options.rationale: This would fit the manic and depressive episodes alone, but it cannot accommodate nine weeks of documented delusions while mood, sleep and function were normal (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, given psychosis outlasting the mood episodes
options.rationale: The defining requirement is delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, with mood episodes present for the majority of the total illness duration, which is exactly the nine week interval documented here (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Schizophrenia with superimposed depressive and manic mood symptoms over four years
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires that mood episodes be brief relative to the psychotic illness, whereas here three full mood episodes dominate a four year course (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Delusional disorder with independent recurrent mood episodes developing separately
options.rationale: Delusional disorder excludes prominent hallucinations and bizarre delusions such as thought insertion, and it cannot be diagnosed alongside episodes of this severity (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder with a secondary recurrent mood disturbance
options.rationale: A negative urine drug screen with a corroborating collateral history of no substance use removes the required aetiological link (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

explanation.summary: The distinction between schizoaffective disorder and a mood disorder with psychotic features rests entirely on longitudinal course rather than on cross sectional severity, which is why it cannot be made at a single interview. Two criteria must both hold for schizoaffective disorder: psychosis persisting two weeks or more without a major mood episode, and mood episodes occupying the majority of the total illness duration. If the mood episodes are brief relative to the psychosis, the diagnosis moves to schizophrenia. The distinction carries real treatment consequences, since schizoaffective bipolar type generally requires an ongoing antipsychotic alongside a mood stabiliser rather than mood stabilisation alone.
key_points: Psychosis for two or more weeks without a major mood episode is the defining schizoaffective criterion
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total illness duration or the diagnosis becomes schizophrenia
The diagnosis is longitudinal and cannot be made from one cross sectional assessment
Thought insertion is a bizarre delusion and excludes delusional disorder
explanation.pearls: Build a life chart plotting mood episodes against psychotic symptoms on the same timeline, because the two week interval of psychosis without mood disturbance is almost never volunteered and is usually recoverable only from dated clinical notes.

subtopic_detail: Autism recognition in adult women previously diagnosed with a personality disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31 year old woman referred after four emergency presentations in two years with distress and self harm. She carries a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder made at age 22 and has completed a full dialectical behaviour therapy program with no measurable change.

Her distress episodes consistently follow open plan office days, unexpected roster changes and shopping centre visits, and settle within hours once she is alone in a quiet room. She describes a stable and consistent sense of who she is, has had one relationship for nine years, and denies any fear of abandonment. She reports rehearsing conversations in advance since primary school and copying the mannerisms of colleagues to appear at ease. Her mother describes lining up objects and intense narrow interests throughout childhood.

data_table.Examination: Reciprocal eye contact effortful and consciously maintained, literal interpretation of questions, no dissociation observed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and urine drug screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat a further course of dialectical behaviour therapy with a different therapist
options.rationale: Repeating a treatment that produced no measurable change without revisiting the formulation compounds the original error, and the trigger pattern here is sensory and predictability driven rather than interpersonal (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Personality Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Personality Disorders

options.text: Commence a mood stabiliser to reduce the frequency of her emotional dysregulation
options.rationale: Mood stabilisers have limited evidence for affective instability in personality disorder and none for sensory driven overload, so this treats a mechanism that is not operating (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Personality Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Personality Disorders

options.text: Diagnose a complex post traumatic presentation and refer for trauma focused therapy
options.rationale: No index trauma is described and the episodes are triggered by sensory and routine change rather than by reminders of a traumatic event, so the required linkage is absent (Source: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health).
source_refs: Phoenix Australia Australian Guidelines for Posttraumatic Mental Health

options.text: Refer for a structured autism diagnostic assessment including a developmental history
options.rationale: Lifelong social camouflaging, sensory and predictability driven distress, narrow interests from childhood and a stable identity together point away from borderline personality disorder and towards autism, which requires a structured developmental assessment to confirm (Source: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia).
source_refs: Autism CRC National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Provide brief supportive contact and discharge her back to her general practitioner
options.rationale: Discharging a patient with four emergency presentations and repeated self harm without revising an unhelpful formulation leaves the recurrent presentations entirely unexplained (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Personality Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Personality Disorders

explanation.summary: Autistic women are diagnosed later and less often than autistic men, and misdiagnosis as borderline personality disorder is among the most common diversions. Camouflaging, meaning the conscious rehearsal and imitation of social behaviour, masks the presentation in clinical interviews and is exhausting enough to be a driver of distress in its own right. The clinical separators are the trigger pattern, sensory and change driven rather than interpersonal, and identity, stable in autism rather than diffuse. Correct diagnosis changes the intervention entirely, moving from emotion regulation therapy towards environmental and sensory accommodation, predictability, and support for the exhaustion that camouflaging causes.
key_points: Autistic women are commonly misdiagnosed with borderline personality disorder
Camouflaging conceals autistic traits during clinical interview and is itself exhausting
Sensory and unpredictability triggers with a stable identity argue against borderline personality disorder
Diagnosis requires a structured developmental history, not cross sectional observation alone
explanation.pearls: Non response to a completed course of dialectical behaviour therapy in a woman with a stable sense of self and no abandonment fear should prompt a developmental history rather than a second course of the same therapy.
